new_statements.quote: Word stress appears not to be contrastive. Stress rules are complex and not fully understood but stress generally falls (a) on each syllable with a phonemic vowel, and (b) on each syllable with a non-phonemic vowel except when that syllable precedes a long syllable, or when it is the second, fourth or sixth syllable in a word that consists only of short syllables. [...] Because single words spoken in isolation carry a contour stress, uttering a word by itself is not a proper test of word-stress placement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: FOR KALAM (not Tai-specific): word stress is non-contrastive and multiple per word — every syllable whose nucleus is a phonemic (half-long or long) vowel is stressed; syllables with a predictable epenthetic vowel are also stressed except when they precede a long syllable, or when they occupy even positions (2nd, 4th, 6th) in a word made up only of short syllables (so all-short words stress the 1st, 3rd, 5th syllables; final short syllables and the first syllable of a three-syllable word are stressed). Weight (phonemic vs epenthetic vowel) rather than position drives placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No primary/secondary distinction is drawn; the source separates word stress (several per word) from phrase or 'contour' stress (about one per intonation unit, not fully predictable, most often on the last syllable of the contour span).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Stress rules are complex and not fully understood'; epenthetic-vowel syllables lose stress before a long syllable and in even positions of all-short words; examples: jakak [ñǰá·γá·k] 'it stood up' (both phonemic-vowel syllables stressed), akl 'bamboo' [á·γɨ́l] (final short syllable stressed), tknak 'you severed (it)' [tɨ́γɨná·k] (first syllable of a three-syllable word stressed).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, but the source says word stress is only observable when the word is inside a multi-word utterance and not utterance-final; citation forms in isolation carry contour stress and are not a valid test. The data are from the Etp mnm of Kaytog (Kaironk) and the Ti mnm of Gobnem-Skow, Upper Kaironk Valley — i.e. Kalam (kala1397), not the Tay/Tai settlements.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog taii1241 'Tai' [taw] = Ethnologue 'Tai (alt. Tay)', Dundrom village, Madang Province (900 speakers, 1990 UBS), NT 2013 by Pioneer Bible Translators. Pawley & Bulmer 2011 (p.14) treat 'Tay (or Tai) mnm' as 'divergent dialects of Ti mnm' — i.e. of Kalam — spoken at Sblap, Fainjur, Dundulom (= Ethnologue's Dundrom), Warabung in the Upper Aunjang Valley, the Middle Asai Valley and the Mjbl Valley down to Anmg near Aiome; Glottolog instead makes Tai a sister language of Kalam (kala1397) under Etp-Ti Kalam (etpt1234). The only stress statement found is the Kalam one (Kaironk Etp mnm + Gobnem-Skow Ti mnm) in that dictionary, already held under kala1397; it is not based on Tay data and should not be filed as a Tai entry.

sources.note: Sec. 3.2.6 (printed p.30): Kalam word stress is not contrastive; stress falls on every syllable with a phonemic vowel and on epenthetic-vowel syllables except before a long syllable or in 2nd/4th/6th position of an all-short word; a separate phrase/contour stress usually falls on the last syllable of the contour span. This describes Kaironk Etp mnm and Gobnem-Skow Ti mnm; Tay/Tai is mentioned only on p.14 as 'divergent dialects of Ti mnm' (Sblap, Fainjur, Dundulom, Warabung, Upper Aunjang/Middle Asai/Mjbl valleys) with no Tay-specific phonological data.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew & Harald Hammarström. 2017. The Trans New Guinea family. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area, 21-195. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. doi:10.1515/9783110295252-002.
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog mada1298). Sec. 2.4.3 'Prosody' (pp.88-89) reviews Donohue (1997) and Ross (2005) on TNG tonal typology (syllable tone, word tone, pitch accent) and states that in languages of the Madang and Finisterre-Huon groups tone and pitch accent are largely absent; contrastive stress is reported only for the Koiarian and Baraic groups. Kalam figures only in the segmental sections (prenasalised stops, predictable vowels). This is the only located printed statement bearing on tone for the group containing Tai; it is secondhand and group-level.

tone.quote: Ross maps the distribution of tonal types in TNG languages of West Papua as follows. In the far west word-tone or syllable-tone systems occur in certain Paniai Lakes languages (Wolani and Moni) and in the disputed TNG isolate Uhunduni. Ekari (Paniai Lakes), Kamoro (Asmat-Kamoro) and the Western Dani languages have pitch-accent prosody. In languages of the Madang and Finisterre-Huon groups and of South-east Papua generally, tone and pitch accent are largely absent.
tone.n_tones: None (tone and pitch accent 'largely absent' in the Madang group)
